script.text: There's a dream I've had since I was small.
I never remember it properly when I wake. Only pieces.
The sound of a river, close by.
Hands that aren't mine, tying a strap around a wrist that is. Slow and careful, like the knot matters more than anything else in the world.
Somewhere above us, a branch moving in the wind.
Petals.
"You're late."
She says it like a complaint. She says it like she's laughing.
She says it like she's been waiting a very long time.
And then I wake up, and the only thing left is a feeling I can't put a name to.
That someone was waiting for me.
That I kept them waiting far too long.
Monday, April 7
My alarm goes off at 5:40.
I'm usually awake before it. I lie there for the full ten seconds anyway, as a matter of principle, listening to the house.
The water heater ticking. A crow on the power line. Nothing from the room down the hall.
Second year of high school starts today. It doesn't feel like anything starts. It feels like Monday.
I get up.
Rice was on the timer last night, so the kitchen already smells like steam. Eggs, the leftover spinach, the last of the frozen karaage. Two lunch boxes, side by side on the counter.
I've gotten fast at this. Fast enough that I can do it while reading the calendar on the wall.
My handwriting is all over it. Kendo: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday morning. Hoshino Kitchen: Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday. A red circle around the eighteenth—Akane's clinic day.
At the bottom of the column, in someone else's handwriting from a long time ago, it still says "Garbage: burnables, Tue/Fri." Dad's writing. I've never written over it.
The fusuma to Mom's room is closed. It usually is.
"Morning."
My sister shuffles in wearing the gray hoodie she's practically lived in since winter, hood up, eyes at half-mast.
"Morning. How'd you sleep?"
"You asked me that yesterday."
"And?"
"And I slept yesterday too. Two nights in a row. Medical science is baffled."
I look at her anyway. Color's fine. She's not leaning on the doorframe. She's not holding her head the way she does when the room starts tilting on her.
"Stop doing the face."
"What face?"
"The doctor face. You don't have a license, Onii."
"I've got an egg with your name on it. That's basically a license."
"I can make my own lunch, you know."
"I'm already making two."
"That's sort of my point."
She says it to the rice cooker, not to me. I decide not to hear it, which I'm also fast at.
The back door slides open. No knock. There's never a knock.
"Good morning. I'm coming in."
"You're already in."
"Then I've arrived. Good morning, Akane-chan."
"Morning, Nanoha-chan."
Tachibana Nanoha. The house next door. Her family and mine have lived three meters apart since before either of us was born.
Our mothers were in the same maternity ward. According to family legend, she screamed louder. According to her, that's slander.
She sets a plastic container on the table.
"Kinpira. Mom made too much again."
"Again."
"Again. She's very bad at measuring burdock. It's a sickness."
It is the fourth time this month that Auntie Emi has been very bad at measuring burdock.
I know exactly what it is. Nanoha knows I know. We both let it be an accident, because the alternative is having a conversation neither of us wants to have before seven in the morning.
"Tell her thanks."
"I will tell her you said it like you meant it."

She goes to the cupboard to the left of the sink—the one with the mugs, not the one with the glasses—and takes down two without looking. She bumps the drawer under the counter with her hip so it doesn't stick. She reaches over the sink and jiggles the window latch at the precise angle it needs, so the steam can get out.
She's been doing all of that since she was tall enough to reach.
Which, considering it's Nanoha, wasn't that long ago.
"I heard that."
"I didn't say anything."
"You thought it in a short-person direction."
"He did. I saw his face."
"Whose side are you on?"
"Hers. She brought kinpira."
"Kō-chan. Your collar."
Before I can do anything about it, she's in front of me, up on her toes, folding my shirt collar back down over my tie.
She has to stretch to reach. She's always had to stretch to reach.
Her hands stay a second longer than the collar strictly needs.
Probably a stubborn crease.
"There. Now you look like someone who has his life together."
"Looks can be deceiving."
"That's why I fix them."
I wrap the lunches. I knock twice on the fusuma.
"Mom, we're heading out. There's rice in the cooker and miso on the stove. Just heat it up."
Nothing.
Then a small shift of weight on the other side of the paper. A creak of floorboard.
That's an answer. Sort of.
The path to school follows the river for a while before it turns toward town.

This week it's the best walk in Shirasawa. The cherry trees along the embankment are at full bloom, so heavy with flowers the branches sag over the path, and every time the wind comes down off the mountains the whole tunnel lets go at once.
Nanoha walks on the river side. She always walks on the river side. I don't remember when we decided that.
"So. Class assignments."
"They'll be posted at the entrance."
"That is the boring answer. I have prepared a theory."
"Of course you have."
"There are six second-year classes. On paper, our odds of being in the same class are one in six."
"However. We have been in the same class for four years in a row. A teacher somewhere has noticed. A file has been opened. There have been meetings."
"Meetings."
"In a small room with no windows. They've realized that if we're separated, something terrible happens. The school's feng shui collapses. The pool turns green."
"The pool is green."
"Because last year they tried to put us in different homerooms for a week during the exchange program. You remember. You were in 1-C for five days."
"That was a scheduling error."
"That's what they want you to think."
I laugh. I can't help it. She has always been like this, and almost nobody knows.
At school Tachibana Nanoha is quiet. Polite. Very good grades, the kind of girl teachers trust with the attendance sheet. People describe her as "gentle." Underclassmen bow to her in the hallway.
None of them have seen her hold a funeral for a goldfish with a full eulogy, a procession, and a small hand-drawn portrait.
None of them know she argues with the TV.
"You laughed. That's two points for me this morning."
"We're keeping score now?"
"We've always been keeping score. You're losing."
A gust shakes the trees. Petals come down so thick it's like walking through snow that forgot to be cold. One lands in her hair, right on the clip, and stays there.
I don't mention it. It suits her.
"Practice today?"
"Club doesn't start until Wednesday. First week."
"And after that?"
"Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday morning. Shifts Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday."
"I know."
"Then why'd you ask?"
"So you'd hear yourself say it."
She doesn't say it like a criticism. She says it like a weather report. That's somehow worse.
"It's fine. I like being busy."
"Mm."
A few steps of nothing. The river is loud this time of year, fat with snowmelt from the Tanzawa.
"Oh. Grandpa says the Ōzakura's the best it's been in years. I'm helping him sweep up there Saturday."
"His back again?"
"His back is a very convenient back. It only hurts on days with a lot of petals."
"I'll come after practice. Somebody has to carry the trash bags while you supervise."
"I do supervise beautifully."
She walks a little faster after that. I have to lengthen my stride to keep up, which, considering the difference in our legs, should be impossible.
The entrance hall is chaos. Two hundred students trying to read six sheets of paper at once.
"Nano-chaaaan!"
A blur with pigtails and approximately nine hair clips hits Nanoha from the side.
"Two-B! You're in Two-B! I'm in Two-B! It's destiny! It's in the stars! I'm going to make us matching keychains!"
"Good morning, Rika-chan."

Hoshikawa Rika. Nanoha's best friend since middle school, art club, a person who has never once used an indoor voice. Today's hair clips: a strawberry, a star, and a small frog wearing a crown. The frog is new.
"And Fujisawa-kun's in Two-B too. Hm. Hmmm."
"What's 'hmmm'?"
"Nothing! Nothing at all. A completely neutral hmmm."
"Statistically, it's a one-in-six chance."
"Tokiwa."
"Fujisawa. We're also in Two-B. I've already chosen my seat."
"We haven't seen the room yet."
"I've chosen it theoretically. Third row, by the window, out of the teacher's natural sightline but close enough to the heater for winter. I made a diagram."

Tokiwa Ryōsuke. Go club. Glasses. My best friend since we were put in the same group for a middle-school science project, which he did all of, and for which he still, unprompted, reminds me he did all of.
He's the smartest person I know and he will spend forty minutes arguing about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. I've seen it. I was there for the full forty minutes.
"Oh! Oh oh oh, but have you heard? Two-B is getting a transfer student!"
"A transfer student?"
"A girl! From—somewhere! Far! I heard she's super tall. Like, taller than the vice-principal."
"The vice-principal is one hundred and fifty-two centimeters."
"So it's TRUE."
While they argue, I squeeze toward the board. I don't make it. Nanoha's already slipped through somewhere at elbow height and is pointing up at a line I can't see yet.
"Fujisawa Kōhei. Two-B. Third from the top."
"You found mine before yours?"
"Yours was easier. It's always right above Fukuda's. Fukuda is very easy to find."
That's not true. Fukuda is in the middle of the list every year. She just looked for mine first.
I don't know why that's the thing that sticks with me all through the opening ceremony.

Tokiwa gets his theoretical seat, which annoys me more than it should. I end up in the second-to-last row by the window. Nanoha's two rows over, which by the standards of the conspiracy is apparently acceptable.
Ōno-sensei, our homeroom teacher, is a tall, tired man who teaches classical Japanese and gives the impression of having been born in a cardigan.
"Alright. Settle down. Before we start—as some of you have apparently already heard through channels I'd like to know more about—we have a new student joining us this year."
"Come on in."
The door opens.
The first thing I notice is her hair. It's impossible not to—a bright, burnished copper, the color of a temple bell in late afternoon, loose and a little wild like she's just come in from wind.
The second thing is that she walks to the front of a room full of strangers like she's walking onto a court she's already won on.
"Mizuno Natsuki! Nice to meet you!"
"My dad's job moves us around, so I've been the new girl—"
She counts on her fingers.
"—six times now? So I'm basically a professional. You don't have to go easy on me."
A ripple of laughter. Someone in the front row actually claps.
"I do kendo. I really, really like horror movies, so if anyone wants to watch one with me, I'll be eternally grateful. And I'm looking for a dojo that'll put up with me. Please take care of me!"
She bows. She comes up out of the bow grinning.
And then she looks straight at me.
For one breath, the classroom isn't there.
There's a smell like rain on cedar. A sound like a river that's nowhere near this building.
And for one breath I am absolutely, completely certain of something that makes no sense at all.
That I've kept her waiting.
Her grin stutters. Just for a second. Just long enough that I'm sure I'm the only one who sees it.
"Sorry—lost my place. Um. That's everything! Thanks!"
More laughter, the friendly kind. The moment folds up and disappears, like it was never there.
I realize I've been holding my pen hard enough to hurt.
"Thank you, Mizuno. Let's see... the empty seat behind Fujisawa. By the window. Fujisawa, raise your hand so she doesn't have to wander."
I raise my hand. She walks down the aisle. When she passes my desk, she slows down just enough to lean in.
"Hey. Kendo, right?"
"...How did you—"
"Left palm. You've got the callus right where the tsuka sits. Takes years to get it that thick."
I look down at my hand like it's betrayed me.
"Takes one to know one."
And then she's past me, dropping into the seat at my back, and I can feel the attention of the entire classroom swing toward the window like a weathervane.
I keep my eyes on the board for the entire first period.
I don't hear a single word of it.
By lunch, Mizuno Natsuki has learned the names of half the class, been invited to two clubs, and agreed to go to karaoke with a group of girls whose names I don't think I've ever said out loud.
I'm impressed. I'm also slightly exhausted just watching.
I've barely gotten the lid off my lunch when a chair scrapes behind me.
"So. You're Fujisawa."
"That's what the attendance sheet says."
"The guy who turned down three confessions last year."
I put my chopsticks down.
"Is that in the welcome packet?"
"Someone told me before I'd finished putting my shoes in my locker! I'm not even kidding! The girl on the left side was very passionate about it."
"Great."
"She said you told every one of them you didn't have time for a girlfriend. Is that true?"
"It's true that I don't have time."
"Huh."
She props her chin on her hand and looks at me like she's reading a scorecard.
"That's either really honest or really sad. I can't decide."
"Let me know when you do."
"I will! I'm very decisive. Usually."
Something about the way she says it makes me want to laugh, so I don't.
"So what rank are you? Shodan?"
"We'll find out on the floor."
"Oh, he's cocky. Good. I hate practicing with polite people."
"Club starts Wednesday."
"Wednesday."
She repeats it like she's writing it on the inside of her wrist.
"Excuse me. Mizuno-san?"
Nanoha's standing by my desk with her lunch held in front of her in both hands, the way she holds things when she's about to do something brave.
"Oh! Hi! You're—"
"Tachibana Nanoha. I sit two rows over. I'm the class representative's assistant, which means I own a clipboard."
"If you'd like, I could show you around after school? The library, the music rooms. Which shoe lockers stick. Which vending machine eats coins. That kind of thing."
For a second Mizuno doesn't say anything. She looks almost startled—like she's not used to being the one who gets asked.
"...Seriously? You'd do that?"
"It's not a big tour. The vending machine part is the most important."
"I would love that. Really. Thank you."
"Oh—and you can call me Natsuki. Is that okay? I'm told I'm pushy."
"...Natsuki-san."
"Ehh, 'san'? We're the same age!"
"I'm working up to it. I need time to adjust."
"Okay, okay. Then I'll just call you Nanoha. Is that alright? I'm going to do it anyway."
"That's—yes. That's fine."
They both laugh. And something about the two of them laughing in the window light, over the top of my head, makes me feel weirdly like furniture.
I eat my rice. It's very good rice. I made it myself.
Natsuki noticed everything.

That was the first thing Nanoha learned on the tour. She noticed that the stairs by the art room squeaked on the fourth step and the eleventh. She noticed the faded rectangle on the wall where a trophy case used to be. She noticed that the third-floor girls' bathroom had a window that looked straight at the mountains, and she said "Oh," very quietly, like she'd been handed something.
"This school's nice. It feels... lived in. Does that make sense?"
"It's very old. The heating sounds like a ghost."
"Perfect. I love it already."

They ended the tour in their own empty classroom, the evening sun coming in sideways and turning every desk gold. Natsuki dropped into Kōhei's chair without asking whose it was, turned it around, and sat backward on it with her arms folded over the backrest.
"So. You and Fujisawa."
"Me and Kōhei?"
"You live next door, right? Somebody said."
"Since we were born. Our mothers were in the same maternity ward."
"No way. So you're, like—real childhood friends. Like in manga."
"Like in manga."
Nanoha said it as lightly as she knew how. She had practice.
"That's really nice."
"I've never stayed anywhere long enough to have one of those. You know? Someone who knows which drawer sticks in your kitchen."
Nanoha didn't say that Kōhei's kitchen drawer stuck. She didn't say she'd known it since she was six.
"Hey. This is going to sound weird."
"I like weird."
"Has he always seemed like... someone you've met before?"
"I have met him before. Every day. For sixteen years."
"Okay, fair! Fair. Forget it. It's the jet lag talking."
"You moved from Sendai. That's barely three hours by train."
"Very intense jet lag."
They both laughed, and the moment closed up, and it was fine.
It was fine.
"Thanks for today, Nanoha. Seriously. First days are usually..."
She didn't finish. She just smiled, and it was a different smile from the one she'd used in front of the class. Smaller. It looked like it cost her something.
"Anyway. Thanks."
Somewhere between the library and the gym, Nanoha had decided that she liked Mizuno Natsuki.
She'd decided it firmly, the way you shut a window against the wind.
She did not let herself think about why it had needed deciding at all.

I'm taking the burnables out to the corner—Monday is not garbage day, but Dad's handwriting on the calendar doesn't know that, and I couldn't stand the bag by the door anymore—when Nanoha comes up the lane with her school bag over her shoulder.
"You're taking out the trash on the wrong day."
"I'm moving it closer to the right day. How was the tour?"
"Good. She noticed the squeaky stairs. Both of them."
"Nobody notices the eleventh step."
"She did."
"She's nice, Kōhei. I like her."
She says it a little too clearly, the way you say something you'd like written down.
"What did you think of her?"
"She's loud."
"You smiled."
"When?"
"When she said she was looking for a dojo that would put up with her. You did your—"
She drops her chin and narrows her eyes and does a frankly offensive impression of what I can only assume is my face.
"I don't have a face."
"You have several. I've catalogued them. That one's number four. 'Somebody wants to fight me.'"
"What's number one?"
"Secret."
She goes up the three steps to her front door. Pauses with her hand on the knob.
"Good night, Kō-chan."
"Night."
The door closes. A moment later, the light in the upstairs window comes on—the one that faces mine, across a gap so narrow you could pass a book across it if you leaned.
I stand there for a while longer than the garbage requires.
That night, the dream comes again.
The river. The branch moving overhead. Hands, tying a knot.
"You're late."
It's the same as always.
Except this time, I almost recognize the laugh in her voice.
Tuesday, April 8
Tuesday is a shift.

Four to seven-thirty at Hoshino Kitchen by the station. Bussing tables, the dish pit, the register when the register needs a body. The manager says "Fujisawa-kun, you're a lifesaver" approximately nine times an evening, which is how I know we're understaffed again.

I get home at eight. I make dinner. I check that Akane did her homework, which she did, and that she ate, which she did, and that she's feeling okay, which she tells me—with feeling—is none of my business.
Mom eats half a bowl of rice in her room. I wash the bowl when she leaves it in the hall.
Nothing happens on Tuesday. That's what Tuesdays are for.

Mizuno spends Tuesday learning the other half of the class's names. By the end of the day she's being called "Nacchan" by three different people and has been offered a seat at four different lunch groups.
She eats with Nanoha and Rika. I know because I can hear Rika from across the room.
Every so often, during class, I feel the back of my neck prickle, the way it does on the floor when someone's measuring the distance between us.
When I turn around, she's always looking at the board.
Wednesday, April 9
The dojo smells like it always does in April: floor wax, old sweat, and the cedar of the walls warming up in the sun after a long winter.
I love it here. I don't say that out loud to anyone, because it's the kind of thing that sounds stupid out loud. But it's true.
Four days a week, for two hours, there's exactly one problem in front of me, and I'm allowed to solve it with my whole body.
"Line up."
Kirishima Aoi, third-year, club captain. She's the only person I know who can make a room go silent by not raising her voice. She's also, as far as I can tell, never once been surprised by anything.
"Welcome back. We have one new member transferring in at the second-year level. Mizuno, introduce yourself."
"Mizuno Natsuki, second year! Sendai Higashi before this, and four schools before that. I've been doing kendo since I was seven. Please take care of me!"

She's in a faded indigo keikogi with the sleeves rolled to the elbow and her hair tied up high and tight. The gi has been washed so many times it's gone soft and pale at the seams. Old equipment. Well loved.
I like her more for that than I want to.
"Fujisawa."
"Takatsuki."
"Nice of you to show up."
"It's Wednesday."
"Yeah. And Tuesdays and Thursdays you're 'busy.' Must be nice."
Takatsuki Shō, second year. We started the club on the same day. He's good—fast, technically clean, and he knows it.
We have never in our lives had a conversation that wasn't an argument wearing a conversation's clothes.
"I have a job."
"I'm sure it's very important."
"Takatsuki."
"...Captain."
He shrugs and steps back into line. I let my breath out through my nose.
It's not even that he's wrong. I miss two practices a week. Everyone knows it. The difference is that everyone else is polite enough not to say it to my face.
I don't know if I respect Takatsuki for that or if I just want to hit him with a stick. Fortunately, this is a club where those are the same thing.
"Warm-ups, then kirikaeshi, then waza drills. After that, jigeiko."
"Fujisawa. You'll take Mizuno for jigeiko. Find out what she has."
"Captain, I can take her if—"
"You'll take the first-years, Takatsuki. They need someone with patience."
"That was a joke."
Nobody laughs. Kirishima seems satisfied anyway.
Warm-ups. Suburi until the shoulders burn. Kirikaeshi down the length of the floor and back, the whole dojo a wall of noise.
Then bogu. The men goes on last—tenugui tied tight over the hair, the helmet settled down over it, the himo pulled and knotted behind my head. The world narrows down to a rectangle behind the grille.
I stop thinking about Tuesday. I stop thinking about anything.
Mizuno faces me across the floor. Through the bars of her men I can see her eyes, and nothing else, and they're bright.
We bow. We step in. We crouch at the line, shinai tips crossing.
"Hajime!"
She explodes off the line.

She's fast. Not fast like Takatsuki, who's fast like a whip—she's fast like water. Everything flows into the next thing. She doesn't stop between attacks, she just keeps coming, and every strike is a question I have to answer.
Men. I parry. Kote. I give ground. Men again—
And then something strange happens.
I know where she's going to be.
Not like reading an opponent. I've done that a thousand times—the shoulder telegraphs, the weight shifts, you guess. This isn't guessing.

It's like a song I learned once and forgot I knew. Her next step arrives in my feet before it arrives in hers. When she drifts left, I'm already there. When she pulls back to bait me, I'm already not taking it.
For a few seconds we're not fighting at all.
We're moving together. Like we've done this before. A hundred times. A thousand.
I think: this is wrong.
I think: no, this is the most right thing I've felt in years.
And because I'm thinking, I'm late—
"Kote-e-e!"
Her shinai snaps down across my right wrist, clean, perfect, with her whole body behind it.
"Kote ari!"
The dojo goes quiet. Somewhere a first-year whispers, "Whoa."
I can hear Mizuno laughing behind her men, a breathless delighted sound.
Something in my chest goes very still and very hot.
We reset.
"Nihonme!"
This time I don't think. I don't wait for the song. She comes in for men and I'm not there anymore—I'm underneath it, stepping through.
"Dō-o-o!"
My shinai cracks across her dō on the way past. Clean.
"Dō ari! ...That's time."
We step back to the line. We bow. I'm breathing like I just ran up the shrine stairs twice.
Mizuno pulls her men off and shakes her ponytail loose, flushed to the ears, grinning like she just won a car.
"You let me have that first point."
"I didn't."
"I know. That's why I'm so happy."
She says it with absolutely no shame. Just pure, clean joy at having hit someone in the arm with a stick. I understand it completely.
"Again next week. Best of five."
"You're on."
"...She's good."
He doesn't say it to either of us. He says it to the floor, grudgingly, like the words were pried out of him with a crowbar.
"Thank you!"
"That wasn't a compliment. It was an observation."
"I'll take it anyway!"
"Mizuno. Good kote. You drop your left shoulder before men. Fix it."
"Ah—yes, Captain!"
"Fujisawa."
"Captain."
"You stopped for half a second in the middle. You were thinking about something. Don't."
"...Yes, Captain."
I don't know how to tell her that I wasn't thinking about something.
I was remembering something. And I have no idea what.
After practice, the first-years usually clean the floor. I usually stay anyway.

It's a Wednesday thing. I can't make Tuesdays or Thursdays, so on Wednesdays I stay late and wipe down the floor and put away the shinai racks and check the bogu shelves. It doesn't make up for anything. It just makes me feel like I've paid something toward it.
Today, Mizuno stays too.
"New member. I'm supposed to do the grunt work, right?"
"First-years are supposed to do the grunt work."
"Then I'm a spiritual first-year. Hand me a rag."

We do the floor the old way—wet zōkin cloths, both hands flat on the wood, running bent double down the length of the dojo and back. She's fast at it. She's also, I notice, deliberately trying to beat me to the far wall.
"Fujisawa! Race you!"
"That's not how—"
She's already gone.
I go after her. Of course I go after her.

The light has gone long and orange through the high windows. The wet floor shines like a river. Our feet slap on the wood and she's laughing and I'm almost laughing and we hit the far wall at the same moment and turn—
Her heel goes out from under her on the wet floor.
I don't think. I'm already moving.
I catch her.
One arm behind her back, my other hand around her forearm, her weight landing in my arms like I'd been expecting it all my life.
For a second, neither of us moves.
Her face is very close. Close enough that I can see the gold flecks in her eyes, the sweat at her hairline, a petal—how is there a petal in here—caught in her fringe.
And for a second, I'm not in the dojo at all.
I'm somewhere outside. There's grass, and the smell of rain. There's someone in my arms, and she's—
—it's gone.
I'm in the dojo. I'm holding Mizuno Natsuki, who I have known for three days.
And she's crying.
Not sobbing. Not anything dramatic. Just a single tear, sliding down from the corner of her eye toward her ear, and her eyes wide and confused, like she doesn't understand where it came from either.
"...Mizuno?"
"Ah—"
She straightens up fast, out of my arms, and swipes at her face with the back of her wrist.
"What—ugh, sorry, sorry. That's so weird. I don't know what—"
"Allergies! It's allergies. Cedar pollen. Kanagawa's full of cedar, right? It's the worst."
"...It's April."
"Late bloomers! Very late bloomers! It's a thing!"
She laughs, too loud, and the laugh echoes off the high ceiling and comes back sounding thin.
I should say something. Anything. Make a joke, let her off the hook.

But there's a pressure in my own chest, right under the sternum, like a hand pressed there. Like I've just put down something heavy I'd been carrying for a long time and my arms don't know what to do now that it's gone.
"...Thanks for catching me, by the way. Good reflexes."
"Yeah. You too. I mean—you're welcome."
"Smooth."
"Shut up."
She laughs again. It sounds more like her this time.
We finish the floor. We don't race.
Her apartment's by the station. My house is the other direction, up toward the hills. The river's where our routes split, so we walk as far as the bridge together because it would be weird not to.
The streetlights are coming on along the railing one by one. The mountains have gone dark blue. Under us the river's catching the last orange of the sky.
"So this is Shirasawa."
"This is Shirasawa."
"It's pretty. Really pretty. I keep thinking I've been here before. Isn't that funny?"
"Have you?"
"Nope. Never been to Kanagawa in my life. Sendai, Niigata, Okayama, Sapporo for like a year, Sendai again. Never here."
"Your dad moves a lot."
"He's good at his job. They keep sending him places that need fixing."
"And I'm good at first days. You saw. I'm amazing at first days."
"You are."
"It's the second semesters I never get to."
She says it lightly. She says it like a joke. She doesn't look at me when she says it.
The river fills up the quiet. A train goes by somewhere toward the station, a bright little chain of windows.
"Hey—so, random thought."
"Mm."
"If you ever want to do extra practice. Early mornings, weekends, whatever. I'm around. Free, even. Not that I'd beg or anything."
She's looking at the river very hard.
"I just mean—it was a good match. I haven't had a match like that in a long time. That's all."
"I work Tuesdays and Thursdays. And Sundays."
"Right. Right, right. Of course. Obviously. You're busy."
"Forget I said anything! It was a spur-of-the-moment thing."
It wasn't. I can tell it wasn't. I can tell she's been carrying it since the dojo, the way you carry a cup too full.
But I don't know what to do with it, so I don't do anything.
"Saturday mornings. Club practice. You'll be there?"
"...Yeah. Yeah, of course."
"Then best of five. Saturday."
"You're on, Fujisawa. You're so on."
She backs away down the far side of the bridge, still grinning, and waves her whole arm over her head like I'm on the other side of a stadium.
"See you tomorrow!"
I watch her go until the copper of her hair disappears under the streetlights.
My chest still feels strange. Like a hand pressed flat there.
Like a promise I don't remember making.
Natsuki got as far as the end of the embankment before she had to stop and sit on the low concrete wall.
She didn't know why. Her legs just stopped wanting to go.
She took out her phone. She opened the chat at the top, the one pinned so long it had its own little gray tab. Chie.
first official kendo practice at the new school
AND???
there's a guy
oh no
not like that!!! he's good. like scary good
he moves exactly how i would move. like he can hear what i'm going to do before i do it
ok that's actually kind of hot
CHIE
also i cried on him
NATSUKI
pollen!!!!!
it's april
why does everyone keep saying that
are you ok tho. for real
Natsuki looked at that last message for a long time.

Chie had been her best friend in fourth grade, and again in eighth grade, when her dad's work had swung them back through Sendai like a pendulum. Chie was the only person she'd ever managed to keep. Two years of messages. Birthday calls. A box of zunda mochi every single New Year, without fail.
Chie was also four hundred kilometers away.
yeah i'm good! made a friend today. a real one i think. she gave me a tour and showed me the vending machine that eats coins
that's my girl
go to sleep. send me pics of the cherry trees
ok ok. night!!
Natsuki put the phone away. She looked out at the river, at the cherry trees black against the last of the sky, at the dark line of the mountains where the shrine was supposed to be.
And a voice in her head said:
"You're late."
It was her own voice. She was certain of it.
She'd never said those words in her life.
Thursday, April 10
Thursday is a shift. Thursday is also, according to the manager, the day I become a mentor.
"Fujisawa-kun! You're a lifesaver. New hire starts today, high schooler like you. Show her the ropes, would you? Register, drink bar, the works."
"Sure."
"Lifesaver!"
That's one.
"Shiina Yuzu, first year at Shirasawa Commercial! Starting today! Please treat me well, senpai!"
She bows. She comes up out of the bow already squinting at me.
"...Ehh? You're my trainer?"
"Fujisawa. Second year at Shirasawa High."
"You look scary, though. You've got dead-fish eyes. Like a guy in a crime drama who's only got one day left until retirement."
"Thank you."
"Do you bite, Fujisawa-senpai? Should I be worried?"
"Only on Thursdays."
"...It is Thursday."
"Then you should be very careful. Register's this way."
"Ooh. He has jokes."
She follows me with her hands clasped behind her back, bouncing a little on her toes, like this whole thing is a game she's already decided she's going to win.

I teach her the drink bar first. Then the dish return. Then the order tablets, which she understands immediately and then pretends not to understand, so that I have to show her again, standing closer.
By the third time, I realize what's happening.
By the fourth time, so does she, and she stops pretending and just laughs at me.
At seven, the dinner rush is over. She leans across the register counter on her elbows with her chin in her hands.
"Senpai."
"Mm."
"If you keep staring at me like that, I'm going to start charging you."
"I'm looking at the register."
"The register is down here."
I look at the register.
"So, senpai. Do you have a girlfriend?"
"No."
"Why not? Ah, wait, let me guess. You're too busy."
"...Did someone tell you that?"
"No! It's all over your face. You have the face of a man who has said 'I don't have time' many, many times."
Between Mizuno and now this, I'm starting to think there's a newspaper somewhere that I'm the main story of.
"But listen. Hear me out. What if you had a girlfriend who worked the same shifts? Then you'd see her all the time anyway. It's efficient!"
"That's not how dating works."
"How would you know? You've never done it."
I open my mouth. I close it again.
"Hehe. Point to Shiina."
Then a man at table six starts yelling.
He's furious about something—the soup, the bill, the drink bar, the general state of the world. I start toward him on reflex, already putting my apology face on.
But Shiina's already there.

"I'm so sorry, sir! Let me fix that right away. Was it the onion soup? Oh, that's my fault—I'm new, and I think I put the wrong ladle in it. I'll bring you a fresh bowl, and there'll be no charge for that today. Would you like a refill on the coffee while you wait?"

She's bright, unhurried, a little apologetic and completely in control. By the end of it, the man is laughing. He leaves her a tip, which nobody at Hoshino Kitchen has ever received in the history of the restaurant.
"Ta-da."
"...That was actually amazing."
"W-what? Don't say it like that. Just normally."
"I'm serious. You're good at this."
"Stop it. That's not fair. You can't just suddenly be nice with that face."
She turns pink right up to the ears. I don't know what I did, but I seem to have won something.
At the end of the shift, at the back door, she pulls her coat on and stops.
"Hey. Senpai."
"Mm?"
"Thanks for being so patient with me today. Really."
And she smiles. A real one, small and quiet.
"...is what I'd say if you'd been patient. You sighed fourteen times. I counted."
She's out the door before I can answer.
Point to Shiina.
It's after ten by the time I get home.
The light's on in the living room. The light's on in Nanoha's upstairs window too. Neither of those things is unusual.
Akane's asleep on the sofa under a fleece blanket, curled up small, one sock half off. The TV's paused on a hospital drama—a surgeon frozen mid-dramatic-sentence.
And Nanoha's sitting on the floor next to the low table, in her house clothes with her hair down, reading one of my manga.
"Welcome home."
"What happened?"
"Welcome home, Nanoha. Thank you for being in my house, Nanoha."
"Did she have a bad day? Did she eat? Did she take her—"
"She ate. She took them. We watched three episodes of a medical drama, and she criticized every doctor in it. One of them she said should be arrested."
I'm already across the room, kneeling by the sofa, the back of my hand going to Akane's forehead. Cool. Normal. Her breathing is slow and even.
"Kōhei."
"When did she come home? Was she dizzy? She was weird this morning, she skipped the egg—"
"Onii. I can feel you hovering."
Her eyes are still closed.
"I'm not hovering."
"Your shadow is on my face. That's the definition of hovering."
She opens her eyes and squints up at me. She looks tired. Not bad-day tired—just ten-at-night tired. Normal tired.
"I got a little dizzy after school. On the stairs at the station. I sat down for ten minutes and it went away. That's all."
"Why didn't you call me?"
"You were at work."
"So? I'd have come."
"I know. That's why I didn't."
It lands somewhere I wasn't guarding.
"I texted Nanoha-chan. She came over. We watched the drama. That's it. It wasn't a thing."
"It wasn't a thing. We only came to the living room because the TV in my house has a much smaller screen, and the surgeon is very handsome."
"He's a terrible doctor, though."
"A terrible doctor. But very handsome."
Two against one. It's always two against one in this house.
"...Next time, call me anyway."
"Next time, don't make a face like I died."
She pulls the blanket up over her head. Conversation over.
Nanoha gets up, closes my manga, puts it back on the shelf in exactly the right spot between volumes five and seven.
"Thanks. For coming over."
"She asked me. I wanted to."
She stops at the door, her hand on the frame.
"Good night, Kō-chan. Window?"
"...Window."
I take a shower. I put the lunch boxes to soak. I do tomorrow's rice.
When I come upstairs, her window's open, and her light's on, and she's waiting.

It's been like this since we were small. Our rooms face each other across the gap between the houses—a gap so narrow that when we were eight, we ran a string between our windows with two paper cups and were deeply disappointed when it didn't work. A gap you could pass a book across if you leaned.
We've passed a lot of books.
I open my window. The night air is cool and smells like wet earth from the hill behind the houses.
Nanoha's leaning on her windowsill in her pajamas, her hair piled up in a bun on top of her head with that enormous pale-blue scrunchie she's had since middle school.
She's holding up a white rabbit plushie with grave ceremony, like she's presenting evidence in court.
"...Who's that."
"Usagi-san."
"I know it's Usagi-san. I bought you Usagi-san. Why are you showing me Usagi-san?"
"He's in time-out."
She turns the rabbit around, slowly and deliberately, so it's facing the wall of her room, and sets it on the corner of the windowsill. Its little tail points straight at me.
"What did he do?"
"We don't discuss it."
"Nanoha."
"He knows what he did."
"He's been in time-out on and off since you were ten."
"He's a repeat offender. It's very sad. The system has failed him."
I lean out and reach across the gap. My fingertips just barely get to the rabbit's ear, and I turn it back around to face the window.
"Kōhei."
"He looked lonely."
"You are undermining my authority."
"Your authority is a plushie."
"My authority is absolute."
She turns the rabbit back to the wall without looking away from me. Her face is perfectly straight. Her eyes are laughing.
This is the version of her nobody else gets. Not Rika, not the underclassmen who bow to her in the hallway. Just me, across three meters of night.
I've always known that. I've just never thought about what it meant.
"...She texted me because she knew you'd leave work."
"I would have."
"I know. That's why."
"That's what Akane said."
"Akane's smart."
The wind moves the trees on the hill. Somewhere down the lane a cat yells at another cat.
"I just—if something happened, and I wasn't there—"
"Then I'd be there. Or Mom. Or Dad. Or Grandpa, who would show up with a broom and a very strong opinion."
"You're not the only person who loves her, Kōhei."
I don't say anything. I don't have anything to say to that that isn't either an argument or something worse.
She lets it sit. She's always been good at letting things sit.
"So. Natsuki-san joined kendo club."
"She took a kote off me."
"She told me. She was very proud. She did a reenactment at lunch. Rika played you."
"How did Rika play me?"
"Badly. She fell over."
"I didn't fall over."
"You're smiling again. Number four."
I touch my own face. I am smiling. Dammit.
"...She's really nice, isn't she."
"She's loud."
"She's nice. And she's pretty. And she's good at the same thing you're good at."
She says it to the rabbit.
"That's a lot of things to be."
"Nanoha?"
"It's nothing. I'm sleepy."
She props her chin on her folded arms on the windowsill and looks across at me. The light behind her makes the loose strands of her hair glow.
"Hey. Those three girls last year."
"Not this again."
"You told them you didn't have time."
"Because I don't."
"Mm."
She turns the rabbit a little on the sill, so it's facing the corner instead of the wall. A reduced sentence.
"What if someone didn't need very much of your time? What if they were already... just. Around. Anyway."
"Then they'd be you, I guess."
I say it the way I'd say the sky was blue. Because it's true. Because she's the only person who's always just been around.
I hear it a second after it leaves my mouth.
She goes completely still. Then very, very pink.
"...Idiot."
"What? What'd I say?"
"Good night, Kō-chan."
The curtain snaps shut. The light goes off.
On the windowsill, just visible through the gap in the curtain, Usagi-san is facing the wall again.
I lie in bed for a long time with the window still open.
I know what it sounded like. I knew while I was saying it. I said it anyway, because it was true, and because saying true things to Nanoha has always been the safest thing in my life.
I lie there wondering when exactly that stopped being a guarantee.
And whether it was ever really one.
Saturday, April 12
Saturday morning practice. Best of five, as promised.

Mizuno takes the first point with a kote so fast I'm not sure I saw it. I take the next two. She takes the fourth with a men that rings my skull like a temple bell, and then she shouts something triumphant through her men that makes Kirishima tell her to be quiet.

The fifth point, the deciding point, we go nearly a full minute without either of us landing anything. It's like fighting my own reflection. Every opening I find, she's already closing. Every feint she throws, I've already read.
In the end, Kirishima calls time. A draw.
Mizuno pulls her men off, sweaty and furious and delighted, and points her shinai at me like a sword in a samurai movie.
"Next Saturday."
"Next Saturday."
Takatsuki watches us from the wall with his arms folded, looking like he's chewing something sour.
I don't think about the strange, easy rhythm of it. The way it feels like a conversation in a language I didn't know I spoke.
I don't think about it at all. I'm very good at not thinking.
The shrine's a twenty-minute walk uphill from our houses. A stone stair through cedars, a weathered torii, and then the trees open up and you're standing in front of the Ōzakura.
The Great Cherry.

People who see it for the first time always stop walking. I've seen tourists do it—the ones who get lost looking for the hot springs and wander up here by accident. They come out of the cedars and stop dead, mouths open.

It's that big. The trunk's so wide three adults couldn't link arms around it, gnarled and mossy and split in places like old stone. The branches spread out over the whole hilltop like a roof. One of them reaches out low and long, almost horizontal, at shoulder height, as if it's offering you its arm.
And in April, every inch of it is in bloom.
Below it, the big flat boulder we used to climb on as kids. Below that, the whole valley: the river, the rooftops of Shirasawa, the mountains folded blue behind.
Nanoha's already there, in her weekend clothes, a bamboo broom in her hands, sweeping petals off the stone path into neat pink drifts.
"You're late."
For a second my heart does something strange.
"...Kōhei? You okay? You went pale."
"I'm fine. Practice went long."
"Who won?"
"Nobody. It was a draw."
"Ooh. You hate draws."
"I don't hate draws."
"You hate draws more than you hate natto. And you hate natto more than you hate Takatsuki-kun."
I can't argue with any of that, so I pick up the other broom.

We sweep for a while without talking. It's a good kind of quiet, the kind we've had a thousand Saturdays of. The wind comes up off the valley and the tree lets go of another few thousand petals, undoing half our work. Nanoha says "Rude" to the tree, very politely.
"Grandpa says it was already this big when the first shrine was built. The records only go back three hundred years, and the oldest one just says 'the great tree.' Like it was always there."
"Maybe it was."
"Maybe."
She stops sweeping. She looks up into the branches.
"When we were small, I used to say a fairy lived here. You remember?"
"I remember. You'd bring her cookies. And then you'd eat the cookies."
"She didn't like the cookies. I was doing her a favor."
"You used to pretend you could see her too. To make me happy."
"I wasn't pretending."
"...What?"
"I never saw her. Not really. But sometimes—it was like hearing someone in the next room. You know? You can't see them, but you know they're there."
Nanoha looks at me for a long moment.
"You never told me that."
"You never asked."
"...I'm asking now. Do you still?"
I open my mouth to say no.
"Whoa. Okay. That's the biggest cherry tree I have ever seen in my life."
Mizuno's standing at the top of the stone path in a navy track shirt and dark sweats, her hair still up in its ponytail from practice, a camera hanging on a strap around her neck.
She's not looking at us at all. She's looking up. Her mouth is a little bit open.
She lifts the camera without seeming to decide to.
"Sorry—sorry. I know, I'm intruding. I just—"
She takes a picture. Then another. Then lowers the camera and just stares.
"I was walking home after practice and I saw the stairs, and I just felt like... I don't know. Like there'd be something up here."
"This is my grandfather's shrine. He's the caretaker. Please, come in. You're welcome here."
"...Nanoha? Wait—and Fujisawa? What are you guys doing here?"
"Sweeping. Kōhei carries the trash bags. I supervise."
"Ha. Yeah. That tracks."
"Would you like some tea? Grandpa keeps a thermos in the office. It's very bitter. You'll hate it."
"Sold!"
Nanoha goes to get it. Mizuno walks under the branches slowly, tipping her head back, turning in a full circle with the camera held loose in both hands.
"You do photography?"
"No. You do?"
"A little. I take pictures of every place we move to. So I have proof I was there. Isn't that dumb?"
"No."
"You say that a lot. 'No.' It's very efficient."
She stops in front of the trunk. She reaches out like she's going to touch it and then doesn't. Her hand just hovers there.
"...It feels like it's looking at me."
I don't say anything. I walk up beside her. I don't know why. The bark's right there, rough and dark and mossy, warm from the afternoon sun.
I put my hand on it.
The hill is the same.
The tree is the same—already enormous, already ancient, the low branch reaching out exactly where it reaches now.

But the shrine isn't there. Just a stone, and a rope. And below the hill, where the town should be, there are thatched roofs and rice paddies flooded silver with spring water, and smoke rising straight up into the still air.
And under the low branch, there's a girl.

Her hair's tied back with a plain cord. Her clothes are faded indigo and old ochre, the kind of thing nobody's worn in hundreds of years. Her hair is the exact color of a temple bell in late afternoon.
She looks back over her shoulder at me, and she smiles like she's been waiting all day just to complain about it.
"You're late."
I know her.
I know her the way you know your own hand.
I'm standing under the tree with my palm flat on the bark. A single petal is stuck to the back of my hand.
My heart's going like I just finished five rounds of jigeiko.
Mizuno is staring at me. She's lowered her camera. Her face has gone pale under the freckles of afternoon light coming through the blossoms.
"...Fujisawa."
"Did you just hear someone?"
"...I don't know."
That's the most honest thing I can say. I don't know. I don't know what I just saw or why I know it or why my eyes feel hot.
"I thought someone said—"
She stops. She rubs her bare arms like she's cold, even though it's warm.
"Never mind. It's the pollen."
"It's April."
"Stop saying that!"
She laughs. I laugh. Neither of us sounds very convincing.
I look around for Nanoha.
She's stopped on the stone path halfway back from the office, the thermos held against her chest with both arms.
She isn't looking at us. She's looking up at the low branch, at a spot just above where my hand had been.
At nothing. At a single drifting point of light, maybe—a fleck of sun through the petals, too bright and too slow, hanging in the air where no light should be.
Her lips move. I can just make out the words.
"...You came back."
"Nanoha?"
She blinks. The light, if it was ever there, is gone.
"Hm? Oh. Nothing. A petal got in my eye."
She smiles. It's a perfectly good smile. I've known her for sixteen years and I'm almost sure it's real.
The tea is as bitter as promised. Mizuno drinks the whole cup anyway and declares it "character-building."
When the sweeping's done and the bags are tied off, Mizuno picks up her camera and her practice bag.
"Okay! I've intruded enough. Thanks for the tea. And the... tree. I'll get out of your hair."
"Natsuki-san. Have you eaten lunch?"
"Eh? Not yet, I was gonna grab something at the konbini by the—"
"Come eat at our house. Mom always makes too much."
"It's a sickness. She's very bad at measuring."
I look at Nanoha. She doesn't look at me.

Mizuno stands there with her bag half on her shoulder. For a second, she looks younger than she did in front of the class on Monday. Like a little kid who's been picked first in gym and doesn't know what to do about it.
"...Really? I can come?"
"You're already invited. It's decided."
"Then—okay! Yes! Thank you! I accept! Oh no, I'm all sweaty from practice—"
"Mom won't care. Sōta will care, but only because he'll want to challenge you to Street Brawlers."
"Who's Sōta? Never mind. I'll destroy him."

The Tachibanas' front door is already open when we get down the hill. Auntie Emi is standing in it in her yellow apron with a wrapped lunch bundle in her hands, as if she'd been expecting exactly this many people.
"Kōhei-kun, welcome home! And—oh! A new friend!"
"Mizuno Natsuki! I'm sorry for barging in—"
"Barging? Nonsense! I made too much. I always make too much. Come in, come in, take off your shoes—Kōhei-kun, this one's for Akane-chan, take it back with you after—"
"Kō-nii! Kō-nii! Street Brawlers! You promised!"
"After lunch."
"You said that LAST time!"
"Oh, Street Brawlers? I main Kagero."
"...Kagero is a coward's character."
"Kagero is a WINNER's character, kid. After lunch. You and me."
"YOU'RE ON."

They disappear into the house, already arguing about frame data. I hear Akane's voice from somewhere—she must've come over already—asking who on earth that is, and Auntie Emi laughing, and Sōta yelling.
Nanoha lingers on the step for a second, looking back up the hill toward the shrine.
"Kōhei."
"Mm."
"...You never answered me. Up there. Whether you still hear her."
I think about the light hanging under the branch. About a girl in faded indigo, smiling over her shoulder. About a voice that's been in my dreams since I was small.
"I don't know yet."
"That's not a 'no.'"
"No. It's not."
She smiles—a strange, soft, private smile that I don't think I've seen before.
"Okay. Then I'll keep asking."
She goes inside.
I stand in the lane between our two houses for a second, in the spring sun, with the sound of everyone in that kitchen spilling out the open door.
Above us, up on the hill, the Ōzakura is in full bloom, the way it is every April. Pink against blue. Perfectly ordinary.
There's nothing strange about it at all.
I tell myself that all the way to the door.
